basics.name: Functional Basis (Stone and Wood 2000; reconciled with the NIST function taxonomy by Hirtz, Stone, McAdams, Szykman and Wood 2002) plus the related Component Basis (Kurtoglu et al. 2005), and the Oregon State Design Repository (OSDR, originally the UMR Design Repository) of products described with them
basics.url: Reconciled Functional Basis, NIST Technical Note 1447 (free PDF): https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=821676 ; NIST record: https://www.nist.gov/publications/functional-basis-engineering-design-reconciling-and-evolving-previous-efforts ; Component Basis (ICED 05 paper, free PDF): https://www.designsociety.org/download-publication/22867/deriving_a_component_basis_for_computational_functional_synthesis ; Design Repository project page: https://design.engr.oregonstate.edu/repo ; its 'alternate link' http://ftest.mime.oregonstate.edu/repo/browse/ did not resolve when tried on 2026-09-25 and has no Wayback copy (see maintained) ; AutoFunc data-mining tool built on the repository: https://github.com/AlexMikes/AutoFunc
basics.resource_type: classification system (a controlled vocabulary of functions and flows, plus a component-name taxonomy) and a digital library / research database of products described with it
basics.cost: Free: the NIST technical note, the ICED 05 component-basis paper and the repository web interface (when online) cost nothing. The journal versions (Research in Engineering Design 13, pp. 65-82, 2002; Journal of Mechanical Design 122(4), p. 359, 2000) are paywalled at the publishers
basics.license: NIST Technical Note 1447 is a US government (NIST) publication, normally free of US copyright [uncertain: it has university co-authors and carries no explicit licence]. The journal versions and the ICED paper are publisher/Design Society copyright (all rights reserved). The repository data carry no stated licence [uncertain]. AutoFunc code is MIT-licensed. The vocabulary (verb and noun lists) is a set of plain words, so it can be cited and re-expressed in our own words, but figures should only be linked
basics.year: Functional basis first proposed by Little et al. 1997 and published by Stone and Wood (1999/2000, J. Mech. Des. 122(4)); reconciled version NIST TN 1447 dated February 2002 and in Research in Engineering Design 13 (2002); Component Basis 2005 (ICED 05, Melbourne). Repository: NSF grant DMI-9988817 (around 2000) at the University of Missouri-Rolla, schema paper Bohm et al. 2008 (Computer-Aided Design 40(7)), moved to Oregon State and still used in papers up to at least 2020 (IDETC 2020)
basics.access_barrier: none for the vocabulary (free PDF); the repository web interface is currently unreachable (host does not resolve), so in practice the product data cannot be browsed today
basics.image_license: Figures in the NIST note and the ICED paper are part of the publications (no separate licence); there are no images of mechanisms as such, only function diagrams and screenshots
basics.authority_level: academic peer-reviewed (NIST, University of Missouri-Rolla, University of Texas at Austin, Oregon State University Design Engineering Lab); the functional basis is the most widely cited function vocabulary in US engineering-design research

coverage.covers: Not a catalogue of connection types but a vocabulary of what parts DO. The reconciled function set has 8 classes (Branch, Channel, Connect, Control Magnitude, Convert, Provision, Signal, Support) with 53 function terms in total, each with a definition and an everyday example (e.g. 'A ratchet joins a socket on its square shaft interface', 'A turnbuckle links two ends of a steering cable', 'A four bar linkage allows a rotational DOF for the trunk lid', 'The gear train of a power screwdriver decrements the flow of rotational energy', 'On a bicycling glove, a Velcro strap secures the human hand'). The flow set has 3 classes (Material, Signal, Energy) with 42 terms. The Component Basis adds 92 standard component names with synonyms and definitions (e.g. Latch = release catch, pawl, lock; Hinge; Key; Magnet incl. electromagnet; Spring; Gear; Cam; Rotational Coupler; Stop = snubber, travel limiter). The repository holds products taken apart and described by component, function, flow and assembly connection: a 2020 study drew 234 products with 7,245 components from it, another used 139 consumer products
coverage.organisation: Hierarchical by function: class (primary), secondary and tertiary terms, plus a 'correspondents' column that maps everyday synonyms onto basis terms (e.g. fasten and assemble map to Join; attach maps to Link; unlock and unfasten map to Allow DOF; hold and fix map to Secure; align and orient map to Position). This synonym table is quite friendly for someone who knows what they want a part to do but not its name. The repository is organised per product (bill of materials of dissected artifacts) with browse and search modes; each component carries a common name, component-basis name, material, functions and connections to other components
coverage.scope_match: medium: it gives a strong, well-defined way to describe connections by purpose (couple, join, link, guide, allow DOF, secure, stop, position, transmit, change/decrement) which suits the flow chart, but it names functions rather than clever connection or mechanism types, and its product data are mostly everyday consumer products, not a list of unusual mechanisms
coverage.taxonomy_used: Functional basis: verb-noun pairs (function + flow) in a 3-level hierarchy. 8 function classes: Branch (separate, divide, extract, remove, distribute), Channel (import, export, transfer, transport, transmit, guide, translate, rotate, allow DOF), Connect (couple, join, link, mix), Control Magnitude (actuate, regulate, increase, decrease, change, increment, decrement, shape, condition, stop, prevent, inhibit), Convert, Provision (store, contain, collect, supply), Signal (sense, detect, measure, indicate, track, display, process), Support (stabilize, secure, position). 3 flow classes: Material (human, gas, liquid, solid, plasma, mixture), Signal (status, control) and Energy (13 secondary types such as mechanical, electrical, magnetic, hydraulic, pneumatic, human). Component Basis: 92 flat component names. Built on Pahl and Beitz function structures and Value Analysis
coverage.example_types: Component Basis names that fit the scope: latch (release catch, pawl, lock); hinge (pivot, pin, dowel); key (half-moon key, cotter key, shear key); rotational coupler (compression coupling, clamping coupling); stop (snubber, travel limiter, bumper); spring (cantilever, coil, leaf, torsion); cam (eccentric, cam plate, camshaft); gear (rack, pinion, ring, sun, planet); pulley and belt; sprocket (chain drive); magnet (incl. electromagnet); screw (lead screw, power screw); link (connecting rod, pawl); lever; guide (v-guide, track, locating hole, jig pin); inclined plane (wedge); rivet (pop rivet); insert (grommet, eyelet, bushing); seal (gasket, o-ring); switch (toggle, flip-flop). Function terms useful as flow-chart labels: couple, join, link, allow DOF, guide, translate, rotate, secure, stabilize, position, stop/prevent/inhibit, transmit, increment/decrement
coverage.making_methods: General product design of electromechanical consumer products (reverse engineering and product teardown); not aimed at 3D printing or any specific making process
coverage.item_count: Functional basis: 8 function classes and 53 function terms; 3 flow classes and 42 flow terms. Component Basis: 92 component names derived from 41 products (1,002 components). Repository: 234 products with 7,245 components used in one 2020 study; 139 consumer products in another 2020 study; earlier summaries cite over 184 products and 6,906 artefacts (search snippet only) [uncertain]
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Only indirectly. Self-locking, hand-release and one-way behaviours appear only through component names (latch/pawl/lock, stop/travel limiter) and function words (secure, prevent, inhibit, allow DOF); there are no terms for torque-limiting, over-centre, indexing/detent, compliant or print-in-place behaviour. Gear trains: yes as a component (gear with sun/planet/ring synonyms) and as the function 'change/decrement mechanical energy'. Powered connectors: magnet (incl. electromagnet), electric motor, switch and solenoid-like 'actuate' functions, and the flow 'magnetic energy' with the example of a magnetic lock. Adhesives: not covered as types (bonding is only implicit in 'couple'/'join')
coverage.entry_structure: Vocabulary entry: term, level (class/secondary/tertiary), definition, one-sentence product example, correspondent synonyms. Component-basis entry: name, synonyms, definition. Repository entry: product, components (common name, component-basis name, material, function-flow pairs, assembly connections to neighbouring parts), sometimes Design for Assembly, human-interaction and environmental data and photos [uncertain for photos]
coverage.audience_level: research and undergraduate (engineering design courses and design-theory researchers)

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: medium for the vocabulary: short plain definitions with household examples (pencil eraser sleeve, turnbuckle, trunk lid linkage, Velcro glove strap), and the correspondents list maps everyday words to the proper term; low for the repository and the research papers, which assume design-theory jargon (flows, function structures, data schema)
usefulness.has_images: few: the papers have function-structure diagrams and screenshots; the repository reportedly held product photos [uncertain]; no mechanism drawings
usefulness.gaps: Says what a part does, not how to build it: no geometry, drawings, design rules, CAD or making advice; no names for clever mechanism types (no ratchet, freewheel, cam cleat, over-centre latch, bayonet or snap fit as distinct entries); nothing on 3D printing, compliant or print-in-place parts; the repository is offline, and its data were never released under an open licence
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: poor: the vocabulary is one PDF with no per-term pages; the repository had per-product pages but the host no longer resolves. Best cited as a whole (e.g. the NIST PDF)
usefulness.reusable_data: Vocabulary: small, can be re-expressed as our own controlled list and cited (NIST publication). Repository: formerly exportable as XML/CSV (AutoFunc reads component, function-flow CSV files mined from it), but no public dataset or licence was found, and the web interface is down, so treat as not reusable today [uncertain whether data files are inside the AutoFunc repo]
usefulness.maintained: Vocabulary: static since 2002 (NIST record updated 2021, still downloadable). Repository: the Oregon State Design Engineering Lab page (copyright 2026) still describes it and gives the alternate link http://ftest.mime.oregonstate.edu/repo/browse/, but that host did not resolve on 2026-09-25 and the Wayback Machine had no snapshot; the older UMR address http://function.basiceng.umr.edu/repository/ is given in the 2005 paper (not opened). Last research use found: IDETC 2020 papers by Oregon State
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Use a short, fixed list of plain verbs for the first flow-chart question 'what should the connection do?': join/couple, link through a middle part, guide or allow a motion (slide, turn), hold in place (secure, position), stop or limit, pass on force or turning (transmit), change speed or force (increment/decrement). (2) Copy the 'correspondents' idea: a synonym table that maps the words beginners type (fasten, attach, clip, lock, unlock) onto our category names. (3) Give every term a one-line definition plus an everyday example product. (4) Keep the two-part description function + what flows through it (force, turning, fluid, signal, electricity). (5) The component basis shows a way to give every entry one standard name plus a synonyms list. (6) Describing each part by what it touches (assembly connections) is a model for a 'connects X to Y' field
usefulness.design_rules_given: no numbers; it is a vocabulary and data schema only
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: No geometry generator. Research tools on the repository: a prototype concept generator (function-to-component matrices), and AutoFunc (Python, MIT) which predicts the functions of components from repository data
usefulness.file_formats: PDF (vocabulary papers); repository stored in a database with XML export viewed as web pages (2005 paper); CSV component-function-flow data used by AutoFunc
usefulness.terminology_value: high for function words and standard component names with synonyms (e.g. latch = release catch, pawl, lock; stop = snubber, travel limiter; rotational coupler = union, compression coupling, clamping coupling); low for names of specific clever mechanisms
usefulness.decision_support: Indirect: the function vocabulary supports function-based concept generation (the repository's prototype concept generator maps required functions to components that have performed them before) and later data-mining tools (decision trees, association rules) that suggest components or functions. No beginner-facing selector, filters or comparison tables
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Builds on Pahl and Beitz function structures, Value Analysis and the NIST Design Repository function/flow taxonomy (Szykman et al. 1999); the Component Basis adopts elements from Greer et al.'s list of 114 components. Overlaps in spirit with Roth's German design catalogues (function-first classification) and with TRIZ/TIPS function lists. Descendants: Repository of Innovative Products (Oman et al. 2014), biologically inspired design keyword maps, AutoFunc
